title: Efficient Assembly of a Defect-Free Quantum Register of 1024 Neutral-Atom Qubits
authors: Lukas Sturm, Marcel Mittenbuehler, Tim Gollerthan, Malte Schlosser, Gerhard Birkl
abstract: Low-entropy arrays of atomic quantum systems in optical tweezers offer unique prospects for fundamental research on few- and many-body systems as well as for extended applications in quantum technology. The significance of this approach relies on the achievable system size, its uniformity, and the rate of qubit allocation. We propel the neutral-atom quantum-technology platform by the rapid assembly of a regular two-dimensional quantum register of up to 1024 atomic qubits, enabled by a novel implementation of intensity-homogenized tweezer arrays and parallelized atom transport. Our highly efficient microoptical architecture modularizes intensity equalization and tweezer patterning in separate functional units, eliminating restrictions that arise for high-power, high-resolution, and large-scale light-field control within a single device. Arrays of precise grid structure, trap depth, and vibrational frequency with more than 3500 sites are demonstrated. Individual sites are interconnected by up to 50 parallelized transport tweezers with intensity and position control in real-time for swift qubit relocation. Multi-tweezer transport enables the operation of target patterns of up to 32 x 32 sites with sustained near-unity filling fraction. These results boost neutral-atom quantum information science above the kiloqubit level.
summary: The research presents an advanced microoptical system capable of assembling massive, defect-free quantum registers using neutral atoms trapped in optical tweezers. By modularizing the trapping array generation and implementing parallelized atom transport, they achieve high uniformity and successfully demonstrate reliable assembly up to 1024 qubits. This significantly advances the hardware capabilities for large-scale quantum information processing.
main_problem: The primary challenge is achieving the efficient, defect-free assembly of a large quantum register containing up to 1024 neutral-atom qubits.
main_result: The authors demonstrated a novel microoptical architecture that enables the rapid and highly uniform assembly of $32 	imes 32$ arrays with near-unity filling fraction, pushing the platform toward the kiloqubit scale.
method: They combine microlens array generation for large-scale trapping with parallelized atom transport tweezers to achieve fast qubit relocation and pattern formation.
model_or_system: The physical system is a quantum register composed of neutral atoms trapped in optical tweezers generated by an advanced, modular microoptical setup. This architecture separates the static trap patterning from the dynamic transport mechanism.

why_interesting: This work directly addresses scalability bottlenecks in neutral-atom quantum computing by providing a robust, highly uniform, and fast hardware platform for creating large qubit arrays.

Large-scale array of atomic qubits forming a quan- tum processing unit (QPU) of 32×32 sites and a surrounding reservoir in an array of 43×43 homogenized optical tweez- ers created by modularized microoptical light field pattern- ing. Inerconnectivity is enhanced by parallelized atomic qubit transport. (a) Single-shot fluorescence image of a defect-free QPU of 1024 qubits. (b) Site-resolved visualization of the cumulative maximum filling fraction for twelve successive re- arrangement sequences. The QPU filling fraction is 99.3(2) %.

Figure 2. (a) Schematic of the optical setup. In two independent input ports, a diffractive beamshaper converts an input Gaussian beam (dashed line) into a top-hat profile (dash-dotted line). Each beam illuminates a microlens array (MLA 1,2) generating a homogenized two-dimensional (2D) array of laser foci. The two resulting static tweezer arrays are combined using a polarizing beam splitter (BS 1) and reimaged into the vacuum chamber. Dynamically steerable 2D parallelized optical tweezers for atom transport are superimposed using a non-polarizing beam combiner (BS 2) with 90 % transmission. The color code indicates the temporal order of parallelized moves along rows and columns within each rearrangement sequence.
